title: Modelling AI’s macroeconomic impact
gist: Oxford Economics models generative AI's macro impact with three adjustable levers (task exposure, adoption speed, labour-augmenting vs. labour-replacing) in its Global Economic Model, landing on a cautious baseline of 3.5%-4.5% US productivity uplift while flagging scenarios where similar GDP outcomes hide very different labour-market and financial consequences.

insights.claim: AI's clearest economic impact so far shows up in capital expenditure, not realised productivity: AI hardware demand has boosted supplier economies in Asia and AI-related spending (hardware, information processing equipment, software) has sustained US business investment over the past two years, while firm-level output gains remain unproven.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Capex-led AI spending can keep boosting supplier economies and equipment/software sales even before any productivity payoff shows up — watch capex data as the leading indicator, not productivity stats.
insights.quote: AI is already affecting the global economy, but the clearest evidence so far is visible in capital expenditure rather than realised productivity gains.
insights.locator: So far, AI's impact has been clearer in investment than productivity

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' baseline forecast is that generative AI makes the US economy about 3.5% more productive over the next decade, rising to 4.5% in the long run — a figure deliberately near the cautious end of a published estimate range spanning roughly 1% to over 12%.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A widely-cited productivity uplift estimate (3.5%/4.5%) is explicitly positioned as conservative versus the broader forecasting community — useful benchmark for judging whether other AI productivity claims are aggressive or in line.
insights.quote: We expect generative AI to make the US economy around 3.5% more productive over the next decade, with the gain rising to 4.5% in the long run.
insights.locator: So far, AI's impact has been clearer in investment than productivity

insights.claim: The gap between rapid AI adoption headlines and limited realised productivity gains is explained by firms needing to redesign workflows and build complementary infrastructure before AI efficiencies convert into higher output — adoption is not the same as integration.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Don't equate AI adoption-rate headlines with near-term earnings upside; the productivity lag implies a multi-year gap between spending and payoff.
insights.quote: businesses still need to redesign workflows and develop complementary infrastructure before the efficiencies created by AI translate into higher firm-level output
insights.locator: Evidence of a broad productivity uplift remains much less conclusive

insights.claim: Oxford Economics built three adjustable 'levers' into its Global Economic Model (GEM) to make AI scenario assumptions explicit: AI Exposure (share of tasks automatable), AI Adoption (share of automatable tasks actually automated), and whether AI is labour-augmenting or labour-replacing.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: This is a reusable mental model for stress-testing any AI macro forecast: separate 'can it be automated,' 'will it be automated,' and 'does automation cut jobs or redeploy them' rather than treating AI impact as one number.
insights.quote: Our model levers seek to answer three key questions about generative AI
insights.locator: Three questions shape our AI outlook

insights.claim: AI exposure is highly uneven by task and geography: clerical, administrative, and IT jobs are among the most exposed to generative AI automation, while physical activities like mining, construction, and fishing are least exposed — so emerging markets with more physical-labour-heavy economies are structurally less exposed to AI disruption than advanced, knowledge-service-heavy economies.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: AI exposure is a country-differentiation factor: advanced, services-heavy economies (and their white-collar labor pools) carry more AI disruption risk/opportunity than resource- or physical-labor-heavy emerging markets.
insights.quote: Clerical, administrative, and IT jobs are some of the most exposed to generative AI in our research, while physical activities like mining, construction, and fishing are least exposed.
insights.locator: How many tasks within the economy can generative AI automate?

insights.claim: AI adoption is modelled as an S-curve that accelerates as the technology is tested and integrated, then slows near saturation; the US is already leading global AI adoption while Japan lags because of a rigid, ageing labour force, and the baseline assumes 80% of possible AI applications are adopted by 2040 across most advanced economies.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Japan's demographic rigidity is flagged as a specific structural drag on AI-driven productivity relative to the US — a country-level divergence to track in productivity/growth comparisons through 2040.
insights.quote: the US is already leading in terms of AI adoption, while Japan lags behind due to a rigid and ageing labour force
insights.locator: How many tasks within the economy will generative AI automate?

insights.claim: Whether AI ends up 'labour-augmenting' (freeing workers for oversight or new roles) or 'labour-replacing' (a net loss of jobs equal to every task automated) is the pivotal unresolved variable that determines whether AI produces sustained growth or structural unemployment; Oxford Economics' baseline bets on augmentation.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The augmentation-vs-replacement assumption is the single biggest swing factor between benign and disruptive AI macro outcomes — track labor-market data (job cancellations vs. redeployment) as the tell for which path is unfolding.
insights.quote: Our baseline view is that AI will primarily augment labour, helping workers perform tasks more efficiently and move into new roles rather than causing a lasting rise in unemployment.
insights.locator: Will generative AI be labour-augmenting or labour-replacing?

insights.claim: In Oxford Economics' 'AI Breakthrough' scenario (faster adoption than baseline), world GDP growth averages close to 3% annually in the 2030s versus 2.4% in the baseline, with the uplift concentrated in the initial adoption phase before fading as adoption approaches saturation.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A faster-than-baseline AI adoption path implies a front-loaded global growth boost this decade that fades later — useful for timing macro/cyclical calls tied to AI diffusion speed.
insights.quote: For the world, annual GDP growth averages close to 3% in the 2030s, compared with 2.4% in our baseline.
insights.locator: What do the scenarios mean for global growth?

insights.claim: The 'AI Disruption' scenario generates productivity gains similar to AI Breakthrough but produces weaker world GDP growth (2.8% vs. 3% in the 2030s) because rising structural unemployment among displaced workers weakens household income and consumption, showing that strong productivity gains alone don't guarantee stronger growth if labour displacement isn't absorbed.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Same productivity gain, different growth outcome: the labour-market channel (job displacement vs. redeployment) can swing GDP by roughly 0.2 percentage points a year in the 2030s even holding productivity fixed — a reminder that consumption/wage data matters as much as productivity data for judging which AI path is playing out.
insights.quote: Structural unemployment rises as displaced workers struggle to move into new roles, weighing on household incomes and consumption.
insights.locator: What do the scenarios mean for global growth?

insights.claim: In the 'AI Disappointment' scenario (slower adoption, weaker productivity gains), world GDP growth falls to around 2.2% in the 2030s, and firms that invested heavily in AI infrastructure face weaker-than-expected returns, which would reduce their appetite for further AI capex and could trigger a reassessment of AI-related equity valuations that dents household wealth and consumer spending.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A disappointment scenario isn't just a lower productivity number — it's a specific transmission chain (weak AI ROI to capex pullback to equity de-rating to weaker consumer spending) worth watching for early signs, e.g. AI infrastructure spending guidance cuts or AI-linked equity multiple compression.
insights.quote: A reassessment of expected returns from AI would also weigh on equity markets, household wealth and consumer spending.
insights.locator: What do the scenarios mean for global growth?

themes.theme: Beyond GDP: Why the Mechanism Matters

insights.claim: Scenarios with similar headline GDP outcomes (e.g., AI Breakthrough's ~3% vs. AI Disruption's 2.8% world growth in the 2030s) can imply very different labour markets, wage paths, and financial conditions, so business and investment planning should look past a single GDP growth number to the underlying scenario mechanism.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: When assessing an 'AI upside' or 'AI downside' growth forecast, ask which mechanism (productivity, adoption speed, labour displacement) is driving it — two similar GDP forecasts can call for opposite portfolio and hiring decisions.
insights.quote: scenarios with similar GDP outcomes may have very different implications for labour markets, consumer demand and financial conditions
